title: Standards in the Preparation of Biomedical Research Metadata: A Bridge2AI Perspective
abstract:
AI-readiness describes the degree to which data may be optimally and ethically used for subsequent AI and Machine Learning (AI/ML) methods, where those methods may involve some combination of model training, data classification, and ethical, explainable prediction. The Bridge2AI consortium has defined the particular criteria a biomedical dataset may possess to render it AI-ready: in brief, a dataset's readiness is related to its FAIRness, provenance, degree of characterization, explainability, sustainability, and computability, in addition to its accompaniment with documentation about ethical data practices.
  To ensure AI-readiness and to clarify data structure and relationships within Bridge2AI's Grand Challenges (GCs), particular types of metadata are necessary. The GCs within the Bridge2AI initiative include four data-generating projects focusing on generating AI/ML-ready datasets to tackle complex biomedical and behavioral research problems. These projects develop standardized, multimodal data, tools, and training resources to support AI integration, while addressing ethical data practices. Examples include using voice as a biomarker, building interpretable genomic tools, modeling disease trajectories with diverse multimodal data, and mapping cellular and molecular health indicators across the human body.
  This report assesses the state of metadata creation and standardization in the Bridge2AI GCs, provides guidelines where required, and identifies gaps and areas for improvement across the program. New projects, including those outside the Bridge2AI consortium, would benefit from what we have learned about creating metadata as part of efforts to promote AI readiness.

This research defines standards for preparing metadata in biomedical research, focusing on "AI-readiness"—the degree to which data can be optimally and ethically used for AI and Machine Learning. The study is crucial because effective AI development hinges on high-quality, well-documented data. Key concepts include FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable), data provenance, characterization, and ethical data practices. This work stems from the Bridge2AI consortium, which generates AI/ML-ready datasets for complex biomedical problems like using voice as a biomarker or modeling disease trajectories. Historically, data collection has often overlooked AI-specific needs, but this initiative provides a systematic approach to ensure data utility.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses the critical problem of biomedical datasets being inadequately prepared for AI/ML methods, leading to suboptimal or unethical model training and deployment. Many datasets lack the necessary metadata—information about the data itself—to ensure their FAIRness, explainability, or traceability, making them difficult for AI systems to use effectively. This research clarifies the specific criteria (e.g., provenance, sustainability, ethical documentation) that render a dataset "AI-ready," bridging the gap between raw research data and its application in advanced AI systems. At TRL 2-3 (concept formulated, experimental proof-of-concept), this provides a foundational framework to guide data generation projects towards AI utility, making complex multimodal data like genomics or physiological measurements usable.

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for AI in healthcare and biomedical research is experiencing rapid growth, driven by the demand for sophisticated diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic tools. This research directly supports this emerging market by providing the blueprint for data preparation, ensuring that investments in AI infrastructure yield reliable results. Industry demand exists from AI developers, pharmaceutical companies, and research institutions seeking high-quality input data. Competitors include various data standardization efforts, but this work uniquely focuses on the comprehensive "AI-readiness" criteria specific to biomedical data. Regulatory hurdles are minimal for metadata standards, and adoption can be accelerated through integration with existing data repositories and Electronic Health Record systems.

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\

Companies specializing in research data management or quantum-inspired data solutions could license or integrate these standards to enhance their offerings. A viable next step involves creating open-source tools or commercial plugins that guide researchers in generating AI-ready metadata from the outset, ensuring future biomedical datasets are immediately usable for advanced AI/ML applications.

title: Whittaker--Henderson smoothing revisited: A modern statistical framework for practical use
abstract: Introduced over a century ago, Whittaker-Henderson smoothing remains widely used by actuaries in constructing one-dimensional and two-dimensional experience tables for mortality, disability and other life insurance risks. In this paper, we reinterpret this smoothing technique within a modern statistical framework and address six practically relevant questions about its use. First, we adopt a Bayesian perspective on this method to construct credible intervals. Second, in the context of survival analysis, we clarify how to choose the observation and weight vectors by linking the smoothing technique to a maximum likelihood estimator. Third, we improve accuracy by relaxing the method's reliance on an implicit normal approximation. Fourth, we select the smoothing parameters by maximizing a marginal likelihood function. Fifth, we improve computational efficiency when dealing with numerous observation points and consequently parameters. Finally, we develop an extrapolation procedure that ensures consistency between estimated and predicted values through constraints.

This research critically updates Whittaker-Henderson (WH) smoothing, a statistical method used for over a century, particularly by actuaries to construct vital experience tables for life insurance risks. The study is crucial because, despite its widespread application in areas like mortality and disability analysis, WH smoothing has lacked a modern statistical foundation. By reinterpreting the technique, this work aims to enhance its practical utility, accuracy, and interpretability by incorporating contemporary statistical principles.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses several key limitations of traditional Whittaker-Henderson smoothing, which impact the reliability of actuarial risk assessments. It introduces methods to quantify uncertainty through credible intervals, provides a principled way to choose data inputs by linking to maximum likelihood, and improves accuracy by relaxing implicit assumptions. Furthermore, it offers a systematic approach for selecting smoothing parameters, enhances computational efficiency for large datasets, and develops a consistent extrapolation procedure. These advancements provide actuaries with a more robust and trustworthy tool for crucial financial modeling.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The actuarial and insurance markets have a consistent demand for reliable data smoothing techniques, making this research highly relevant. Companies constructing mortality, disability, and other risk tables would benefit significantly from the enhanced accuracy and statistical rigor provided. While existing WH implementations are competitors, this modern framework offers a clear advantage through its improved precision, uncertainty quantification, and efficiency. Adopting these advancements could lead to more confident risk pricing and compliance, though integrating new methodologies into legacy systems might require initial investment.

While the underlying statistical theory might not be patentable, specific algorithmic implementations for improved computational efficiency or the novel extrapolation procedure could be. title: Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails: Real World Preasymptotics, Epistemology, and Applications
abstract:
(The third edition corrects minor typos and adds 3 chapters synthesized from published papers plus an appendix on maximum entropy distributions.) The monograph investigates the misapplication of conventional statistical techniques to fat tailed distributions and looks for remedies, when possible.
  Switching from thin tailed to fat tailed distributions requires more than "changing the color of the dress". Traditional asymptotics deal mainly with either n=1 or $n=\infty$, and the real world is in between, under of the "laws of the medium numbers" --which vary widely across specific distributions. Both the law of large numbers and the generalized central limit mechanisms operate in highly idiosyncratic ways outside the standard Gaussian or Levy-Stable basins of convergence.
  A few examples:
  + The sample mean is rarely in line with the population mean, with effect on "naive empiricism", but can be sometimes be estimated via parametric methods.
  + The "empirical distribution" is rarely empirical.
  + Parameter uncertainty has compounding effects on statistical metrics.
  + Dimension reduction (principal components) fails.
  + Inequality estimators (GINI or quantile contributions) are not additive and produce wrong results.
  + Many "biases" found in psychology become entirely rational under more sophisticated probability distributions
  + Most of the failures of financial economics, econometrics, and behavioral economics can be attributed to using the wrong distributions.
  This book, the first volume of the Technical Incerto, weaves a narrative around published journal articles.

This research critically examines the implications of "fat-tailed" statistical distributions, which are prevalent in the real world but often overlooked by conventional statistical methods. It investigates why traditional asymptotic theories, designed for ideal scenarios, fail when applied to real-world data, highlighting the fundamental differences between theoretical assumptions and practical observations. Understanding these "laws of the medium numbers" is crucial because many phenomena, from financial markets to natural disasters, exhibit extreme events more frequently than standard models predict, leading to significant miscalculations and flawed interpretations.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses the widespread problem of misinterpreting data by demonstrating how standard statistical tools—like sample means, empirical distributions, or dimension reduction techniques—produce inaccurate and misleading results when applied to fat-tailed datasets. It explains why common assumptions, such as the Law of Large Numbers or the Central Limit Theorem, behave idiosyncratically outside idealized conditions, leading to failures in fields such as financial economics, econometrics, and behavioral science. At TRL 2 (concept formulated), this theoretical framework provides a vital explanation for observed model failures and offers a basis for developing more robust analytical approaches.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for robust statistical methods is substantial and spans finance, insurance, risk management, and any data-driven industry where understanding extreme events is critical. There is significant demand for tools that can accurately model real-world uncertainty, as current industry practices often underestimate risks due to reliance on inappropriate statistical assumptions. While existing statistical software offers many features, this research identifies a core conceptual gap that, if addressed, could lead to more reliable forecasting and decision-making. Overcoming the inertia of established methods and educating practitioners about these fundamental distinctions are key challenges, but collaborations with data analytics platforms could accelerate adoption.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This research, by exposing mathematical consequences rather than creating an invention, is unlikely to be patentable itself. However, it provides foundational insights for developing new software and services. A viable startup could emerge by creating specialized statistical software libraries or consulting services that specifically design and implement models robust to fat-tailed distributions, particularly for risk assessment in finance or insurance. title: A primal-dual price-optimization method for computing equilibrium prices in mean-field games models
abstract: We develop a simple yet efficient Lagrangian method for computing equilibrium prices in a mean-field game price-formation model. We prove that equilibrium prices are optimal in terms of a suitable criterion and derive a primal-dual gradient-based algorithm for computing them. One of the highlights of our computational framework is the efficient, simple, and flexible implementation of the algorithm using modern automatic differentiation techniques. Our implementation is modular and admits a seamless extension to high-dimensional settings with more complex dynamics, costs, and equilibrium conditions. Additionally, automatic differentiation enables a versatile algorithm that requires only coding the cost functions of agents. It automatically handles the gradients of the costs, thereby eliminating the need to manually form the adjoint equations.

title: Valuation of Exotic Options and Counterparty Games Based on Conditional Diffusion
abstract: This paper addresses the challenges of pricing exotic options and structured products, which traditional models often fail to handle due to their inability to capture real-world market phenomena like fat-tailed distributions and volatility clustering. We introduce a Diffusion-Conditional Probability Model (DDPM) to generate more realistic price paths. Our method incorporates a composite loss function with financial-specific features, and we propose a P-Q dynamic game framework for evaluating the model's economic value through adversarial backtesting. Static validation shows our P-model effectively matches market mean and volatility. In dynamic games, it demonstrates significantly higher profitability than a traditional Monte Carlo-based model for European and Asian options. However, the model shows limitations in pricing products highly sensitive to extreme events, such as snowballs and accumulators, because it tends to underestimate tail risks. The study concludes that diffusion models hold significant potential for enhancing pricing accuracy, though further research is needed to improve their ability to model extreme market risks.

The study introduces a novel Diffusion-Conditional Probability Model (DDPM) to generate more realistic market price paths, thereby enhancing the precision of financial risk assessment and product valuation.

title: Land and Infinite Debt Rollover
abstract: Since McCallum (1987), it is well known that in an overlapping generations (OLG) economy with land, the equilibrium is Pareto efficient because with balanced growth, the interest rate exceeds the economic growth rate ($R>G$), which rules out infinite debt rollover (a Ponzi scheme). title: Canonical correlation analysis of stochastic trends via functional approximation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for semiparametric inference on the number $s$ of common trends and their loading matrix $ψ$ in $I(1)/I(0)$ systems. It combines functional approximation of limits of random walks and canonical correlations analysis, performed between the $p$ observed time series of length $T$ and the first $K$ discretized elements of an $L^2$ basis. Tests and selection criteria on $s$, and estimators and tests on $ψ$ are proposed; their properties are discussed as $T$ and $K$ diverge sequentially for fixed $p$ and $s$. It is found that tests on $s$ are asymptotically pivotal, selection criteria of $s$ are consistent, estimators of $ψ$ are $T$-consistent, mixed-Gaussian and efficient, so that Wald tests on $ψ$ are asymptotically Normal or $χ^2$. The paper also discusses asymptotically pivotal misspecification tests for checking model assumptions. The approach can be coherently applied to subsets or aggregations of variables in a given panel. Monte Carlo simulations show that these tools have reasonable performance for $T\geq 10 p$ and $p\leq 300$. An empirical analysis of 20 exchange rates illustrates the methods.

title: Robotic modeling of snake traversing large, smooth obstacles reveals stability benefits of body compliance
abstract: Snakes can move through almost any terrain. Although their locomotion on flat surfaces using planar gaits is inherently stable, when snakes deform their body out of plane to traverse complex terrain, maintaining stability becomes a challenge. On trees and desert dunes, snakes grip branches or brace against depressed sand for stability. However, how they stably surmount obstacles like boulders too large and smooth to gain such anchor points is less understood. Similarly, snake robots are challenged to stably traverse large, smooth obstacles for search and rescue and building inspection. Our recent study discovered that snakes combine body lateral undulation and cantilevering to stably traverse large steps. Here, we developed a snake robot with this gait and snake-like anisotropic friction and used it as a physical model to understand stability principles. The robot traversed steps as high as a third of its body length rapidly and stably. However, on higher steps, it was more likely to fail due to more frequent rolling and flipping over, which was absent in the snake with a compliant body. Adding body compliance reduced the robot roll instability by statistically improving surface contact, without reducing speed. Besides advancing understanding of snake locomotion, our robot achieved high traversal speed surpassing most previous snake robots and approaching snakes, while maintaining high traversal probability.

title: Graph Signal Processing for Global Stock Market Realized Volatility Forecasting
abstract: This paper introduces an innovative realized volatility (RV) forecasting framework that extends the conventional Heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) model via integrating Graph Signal Processing (GSP). The study first evaluates various constructions of volatility-interrelationship networks by analyzing how the associated graph signal energy tracks global financial market volatility. Volatility spillovers are subsequently embedded into the proposed framework, which employs the graph Fourier transform (GFT) and its inverse to effectively capture global stock market dynamics in both the spectral and spatial domains. The framework not only provides a global context for modeling the volatility interrelationships, but also captures the nonlinearity and directionality of the volatility spillover effect. The empirical study using RV data of $24$ global stock market indices compares short-, mid- and long-term RV forecasts with various HAR-type benchmarks and a graph neural network-based HAR model. The proposed model consistently outperforms all comparators, demonstrating the effectiveness of integrating GSP into the HAR model for RV forecasting.

title: Trial Length, Pricing, and Rationally Inattentive Customers
abstract: The "free trial" followed by automatic renewal is a dominant business model in the digital economy. Standard models explain trials as a mechanism for consumers to learn their valuation for a product. We propose a complementary theory based on the rational inattention framework. Consumers know their valuation but face a cognitive cost to remember to cancel an unwanted subscription. We model this using a Shannon entropy-based cost of information processing, where a consumer's baseline attention level decays with the length of the trial period. This creates a novel trade-off for a monopolist firm: a longer trial increases "inattentive revenue" from consumers who fail to cancel, but it also lowers ex-ante consumer utility, making the initial offer less attractive. We show that this trade-off leads to an interior optimal trial length, even for products where value-learning is instantaneous. Our model, under standard assumptions about demand elasticity and the distribution of consumer valuations, generates sharp, testable predictions about the relationship between contract terms. We find that the optimal renewal price and trial length are complements: firms offering longer trials will also set higher post-trial prices. We analyze the impact of policies aimed at curbing consumer exploitation, such as "click-to-cancel" regulations. We show that such policies, by making attention effectively cheaper, lead firms to reduce trial lengths. The effect on price depends directly on the elasticity of demand from loyal subscribers. We also extend the model to include paid trials, showing that introductory prices and trial lengths act as strategic substitutes. Our framework provides a micro-founded explanation for common features of subscription contracts and offers a new lens through which to evaluate consumer protection policies in digital markets.

title: BIM-to-BRICK: Using graph modeling for IoT/BMS and spatial semantic data interoperability within digital data models of buildings
abstract: The holistic management of a building requires data from heterogeneous sources such as building management systems (BMS), Internet-of-Things (IoT) sensor networks, and building information models. Data interoperability is a key component to eliminate silos of information, and using semantic web technologies like the BRICK schema, an effort to standardize semantic descriptions of the physical, logical, and virtual assets in buildings and the relationships between them, is a suitable approach. However, current data integration processes can involve significant manual interventions. This paper presents a methodology to automatically collect, assemble, and integrate information from a building information model to a knowledge graph. The resulting application, called BIM-to-BRICK, is run on the SDE4 building located in Singapore. BIM-to-BRICK generated a bidirectional link between a BIM model of 932 instances and experimental data collected for 17 subjects into 458 BRICK objects and 1219 relationships in 17 seconds. The automation of this approach can be compared to traditional manual mapping of data types. This scientific innovation incentivizes the convergence of disparate data types and structures in built-environment applications.

title: Dynamic Inverse Optimization under Drift and Shocks: Theory, Regret Bounds, and Applications
abstract: The growing prevalence of drift and shocks in modern decision environments exposes a gap between classical optimization theory and real-world practice. Standard models assume fixed objectives, yet organizations from hospitals to power grids routinely adapt to shifting priorities, noisy data, and abrupt disruptions. To address this gap, this study develops a dynamic inverse optimization framework that recovers hidden, time-varying preferences from observed allocation trajectories. The framework unifies identifiability analysis with regret guarantees conditions are established for existence and uniqueness of recovered parameters, and sharp static and dynamic regret bounds are derived to characterize responsiveness to gradual drift and sudden shocks. Methodologically, a drift-aware estimator grounded in convex analysis and online learning theory is introduced, with finite-sample guarantees on recovery accuracy. Computational experiments in healthcare, energy, logistics, and finance reveal heterogeneous recovery patterns, ranging from rapid resilience to persistent vulnerability. Overall, dynamic inverse optimization emerges as both a theoretical contribution and a broadly applicable diagnostic tool for benchmarking resilience, uncovering hidden behavioral shifts, and guiding policy interventions in complex stochastic systems.

\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research addresses a critical gap between classical optimization theory, which assumes fixed goals, and the reality of modern decision environments. Organizations from hospitals to power grids constantly adapt to shifting priorities, noisy data, and abrupt disruptions—phenomena referred to as "drift and shocks." This study introduces a dynamic inverse optimization framework to recover these hidden, time-varying preferences from observed operational choices and allocation trajectories. It is crucial for understanding how complex systems truly adapt and identifying the underlying reasons for their actions when facing dynamic, uncertain conditions.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper solves the problem of understanding *why* decisions are made in dynamic environments where objectives are not static but evolve due to gradual "drift" or sudden "shocks." It provides a systematic way to infer these changing underlying preferences from observed actions, offering a diagnostic tool to assess organizational resilience and vulnerability. At TRL 2 (concept formulated), this theoretical framework clarifies the limitations of static models and provides rigorous methods (identifiability analysis, regret bounds) to quantify how well hidden preferences can be recovered. Advancing this work requires applying the framework to extensive real-world datasets for empirical validation in specific sectors.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for understanding and optimizing complex systems under uncertainty is vast, spanning healthcare resource allocation, energy grid management, logistics, and financial trading. Industry demand exists for tools that can benchmark organizational resilience and uncover behavioral shifts that impact performance. This research offers a unique analytical lens that goes beyond traditional optimization, identifying dynamic preferences. Adoption challenges include the need for extensive historical data on decisions and outcomes, as well as integrating this advanced analytical framework into existing decision-support systems. Competitors are primarily static optimization software or heuristic decision models, but this work provides a more nuanced, dynamic approach.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This research develops a fundamental analytical framework rather than a directly patentable invention. However, it strongly informs the development of advanced diagnostic and decision-support tools. Startups could build specialized software platforms that implement this dynamic inverse optimization framework for specific industries (e.g., healthcare capacity planning, energy portfolio management) to help organizations understand their own adaptive strategies and benchmark resilience. Consulting firms might license the methodology to offer services focused on uncovering hidden organizational preferences and guiding policy interventions. A practical next step involves creating open-source libraries or commercial software modules that enable data scientists to apply this framework to their organizational datasets.

title: Blind Network Revenue Management and Bandits with Knapsacks under Limited Switches
abstract: This paper studies the impact of limited switches on resource-constrained dynamic pricing with demand learning. We focus on the classical price-based blind network revenue management problem and extend our results to the bandits with knapsacks problem. In both settings, a decision maker faces stochastic and distributionally unknown demand, and must allocate finite initial inventory across multiple resources over time. In addition to standard resource constraints, we impose a switching constraint that limits the number of action changes over the time horizon. We establish matching upper and lower bounds on the optimal regret and develop computationally efficient limited-switch algorithms that achieve it. We show that the optimal regret rate is fully characterized by a piecewise-constant function of the switching budget, which further depends on the number of resource constraints. Our results highlight the fundamental role of resource constraints in shaping the statistical complexity of online learning under limited switches. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our algorithms maintain strong cumulative reward performance while significantly reducing the number of switches.

title: Deep Learning in the Sequence Space
abstract: We develop a deep learning algorithm for approximating functional rational expectations equilibria of dynamic stochastic economies in the sequence space. We use deep neural networks to parameterize equilibrium objects of the economy as a function of truncated histories of exogenous shocks. We train the neural networks to fulfill all equilibrium conditions along simulated paths of the economy. To illustrate the performance of our method, we solve three economies of increasing complexity: the stochastic growth model, a high-dimensional overlapping generations economy with multiple sources of aggregate risk, and finally an economy where households and firms face uninsurable idiosyncratic risk, shocks to aggregate productivity, and shocks to idiosyncratic and aggregate volatility. Furthermore, we show how to design practical neural policy function architectures that guarantee monotonicity of the predicted policies, facilitating the use of the endogenous grid method to simplify parts of our algorithm.
